items.stem: What is a class?
options: A single instance of an object
A template (blueprint) that defines the attributes and methods of a type of object
A variable that holds a number
A subroutine that returns a value
items.answer: A template (blueprint) that defines the attributes and methods of a type of object
items.markingKey: Objects are instances of a class.

items.stem: Explain how encapsulation helps to keep an object's data valid.
items.answer: Attributes are private, so the only way to change them is through public methods, which can check (validate) new values before changing the data.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Explain the difference between a class and an object.
items.answer: A class is the definition/template of attributes and methods; an object is a particular instance created from the class with its own attribute values.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem:
The class is defined:
CLASS SavingsPot
    PRIVATE Saved : INTEGER
    PUBLIC PROCEDURE NEW(Start : INTEGER)
        Saved ← Start
    ENDPROCEDURE
    PUBLIC PROCEDURE Deposit(Amount : INTEGER)
        Saved ← Saved + Amount
    ENDPROCEDURE
    PUBLIC FUNCTION Withdraw(Amount : INTEGER) RETURNS BOOLEAN
        IF Amount <= Saved THEN
            Saved ← Saved - Amount
            RETURN TRUE
        ELSE
            RETURN FALSE
        ENDIF
    ENDFUNCTION
    PUBLIC FUNCTION GetSaved() RETURNS INTEGER
        RETURN Saved
    ENDFUNCTION
ENDCLASS
The main program is:
Acc ← NEW SavingsPot(200)
OUTPUT Acc.Withdraw(170)
CALL Acc.Deposit(20)
OUTPUT Acc.GetSaved()
OUTPUT Acc.GetSaved()
State the output of the main program.
items.answer: TRUE 50 50
items.markingKey: Withdraw returns FALSE and leaves Saved unchanged if Amount > Saved; outputs TRUE, 50, 50 [3]

items.stem: GreenLeaf Pharmacy in Mumbai is writing an object-oriented system to manage customer accounts. (a) Explain the difference between a class and an object in this system. (b) Describe two benefits of using OOP for this system.
items.answer: (a) Class: the template for all accounts; object: one particular account with its own balance. (b) Encapsulation protects data; classes can be reused/inherited; easier maintenance; models real-world entities.

items.stem: What is an object?
options: A data type such as INTEGER
A method of a class
An instance of a class
A template for creating classes
items.answer: An instance of a class
items.markingKey: Created with NEW; has its own attribute values.

items.stem: What is encapsulation?
options: Using one method name for different actions
Storing objects in a file
Creating a new class from an existing class
Combining data and the methods that act on it in one class, and hiding the data from outside access
items.answer: Combining data and the methods that act on it in one class, and hiding the data from outside access
items.markingKey: Attributes are PRIVATE; access is through PUBLIC methods.

items.stem: Assertion (A): Private attributes can be accessed from anywhere in the program. Reason (R): Encapsulation restricts access to the methods of the class. Which option is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
items.answer: A is false but R is true
items.markingKey: A is false: "Private attributes can be accessed from anywhere in the program." is incorrect; R is a true statement.

items.stem: What is a constructor?
options: A method that is called when an object is created, to initialise its attributes
A method that deletes an object
A method that returns an attribute
A class with no methods
items.answer: A method that is called when an object is created, to initialise its attributes
items.markingKey: In Cambridge pseudocode it is PROCEDURE NEW(...).

items.stem: Explain why setters are used instead of making attributes public.
items.answer: A setter can validate the new value before changing the private attribute, so invalid data cannot be stored; the internal representation can change without affecting other code.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Explain why a constructor is needed.
items.answer: It makes sure every new object starts in a valid state with all attributes initialised (possibly from parameters).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Write pseudocode for a class Room for Coral Bay Aquarium with the private attributes RoomNumber : INTEGER, Capacity : INTEGER, Booked : BOOLEAN, a constructor that sets all the attributes from parameters, a getter for RoomNumber and a setter for Capacity. The setter for Capacity must only accept values from 0 to 1000 and return TRUE or FALSE.
items.answer:
CLASS Room
    PRIVATE RoomNumber : INTEGER
    PRIVATE Capacity : INTEGER
    PRIVATE Booked : BOOLEAN
    PUBLIC PROCEDURE NEW(pRoomNumber : INTEGER, pCapacity : INTEGER, pBooked : BOOLEAN)
        RoomNumber ← pRoomNumber
        Capacity ← pCapacity
        Booked ← pBooked
    ENDPROCEDURE
    PUBLIC FUNCTION GetRoomNumber() RETURNS INTEGER
        RETURN RoomNumber
    ENDFUNCTION
    PUBLIC FUNCTION SetCapacity(NewCapacity : INTEGER) RETURNS BOOLEAN
        IF NewCapacity >= 0 AND NewCapacity <= 1000 THEN
            Capacity ← NewCapacity
            RETURN TRUE
        ELSE
            RETURN FALSE
        ENDIF
    ENDFUNCTION
ENDCLASS
items.markingKey: 1 mark CLASS/ENDCLASS with PRIVATE attributes; 1 mark constructor NEW with parameters; 1 mark assignments; 1 mark getter; 1 mark setter with validation and return [5]

items.stem: What is inheritance?
options: Creating a new (derived) class that takes on the attributes and methods of an existing (base) class
Storing one object inside another
Using the same name for different methods in one class
Hiding data inside a class
items.answer: Creating a new (derived) class that takes on the attributes and methods of an existing (base) class
items.markingKey: CLASS Car INHERITS Vehicle.

items.stem: Explain how inheritance reduces the amount of code a programmer writes.
items.answer: Common attributes and methods are written once in the base class and reused by every derived class, which only adds or overrides what is different.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Explain the difference between polymorphism and overloading.
items.answer: Polymorphism: a derived class redefines (overrides) an inherited method with the same signature; overloading: several methods in one class share a name but have different parameters.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem:
A base class Shape has a method Area() that is overridden in each derived class:
CLASS Shape
    PUBLIC FUNCTION Area() RETURNS REAL
        RETURN 0
    ENDFUNCTION
ENDCLASS
CLASS Rectangle INHERITS Shape  // NEW(W, H); Area() RETURNS W * H
CLASS Circle INHERITS Shape  // NEW(R); Area() RETURNS 3.142 * R * R
CLASS Triangle INHERITS Shape  // NEW(B, H); Area() RETURNS 0.5 * B * H
The main program is:
Shape1 ← NEW Triangle(2, 14)
Shape2 ← NEW Circle(7)
OUTPUT Shape1.Area()
OUTPUT Shape2.Area()
State the output and explain why Shape.Area() is not used.
items.answer: 14 153.958; each derived class overrides Area() (polymorphism), so the version for the object's own class runs.

ENDCLASS
CLASS Manager INHERITS Employee
    PRIVATE Bonus : INTEGER
    PUBLIC PROCEDURE NEW(R : INTEGER, H : INTEGER, B : INTEGER)
        SUPER.NEW(R, H)
        Bonus ← B
    ENDPROCEDURE
    PUBLIC FUNCTION Pay() RETURNS INTEGER
        RETURN SUPER.Pay() + Bonus
    ENDFUNCTION
ENDCLASS
Zara ← NEW Employee(28, 39)
Sofia ← NEW Manager(17, 25, 170)
OUTPUT Zara.Pay()
OUTPUT Sofia.Pay()
State the output and identify where inheritance and polymorphism are used. (b) A Department class holds an array of Employee objects. Identify this relationship and explain one benefit.
items.answer: (a) 1092 595; Manager INHERITS Employee (inheritance); Pay() is overridden in Manager (polymorphism), which calls SUPER.Pay(). (b) Containment/aggregation ("has a"): the department can process all its staff together (e.g. total pay) while each Employee remains a separate object.
items.markingKey: (a) 28 × 39 = 1092 [1]; 17 × 25 + 170 = 595 [1]; inheritance [1]; polymorphism [1] [4] (b) 1 mark relationship; 1 mark benefit [2]
